Seminar Title:

Seismic Bearing and Uplift Capacity of Strip Footings and Anchors near Soil Slopes using Lower Bound Limit Analysis

Seminar Type:

Synopsis Seminar

Department:

Civil Engineering

Speaker Name:

Neelagiri Vallaba Datta ( Rollno : 521ce1019)

Speaker Type:

Student

Venue:

Department Seminar Room (CE)

Date and Time:

09 Nov 2026 5:15 PM

Contact:

Sunil Khuntia

Abstract:

Foundations of transmission towers, hydropower facilities, hill roads and buildings in hilly regions are frequently placed on or close to sloping ground, where the reduced confinement offered by the slope and the inertial forces induced by earthquakes can markedly lower the bearing resistance of footings and the uplift resistance of anchors. Existing solutions for such problems mostly rely on assumed failure mechanisms, represent earthquake loading through the pseudo-static approach, and evaluate the contributions of cohesion and soil unit weight separately through the principle of superposition. The present thesis addresses these limitations by evaluating the seismic bearing capacity of strip footings and the seismic uplift capacity of strip anchors located near soil slopes.
Four problems are examined: (i) a strip footing placed beyond the crest of a cohesive&ndashfrictional slope, (ii) a strip anchor embedded beyond the crest of a cohesionless slope, (iii) a strip anchor embedded beyond the crest of a cohesive&ndashfrictional slope and (iv) a strip anchor embedded beneath the inclined face of a cohesive&ndashfrictional slope. The solutions are obtained using lower bound finite element limit analysis in combination with second-order cone programming, in which the Mohr&ndashCoulomb criterion is represented exactly and no failure mechanism is assumed in advance. The seismic body forces are incorporated through the modified pseudo-dynamic method, which accounts for the propagation of shear and primary waves, soil damping and the amplification of ground motion, and the horizontal seismic acceleration is assigned to each element according to its depth. For cohesive&ndashfrictional soils, cohesion, internal friction and unit weight are considered simultaneously through single combined capacity factors (Nc&gammas and Fc&gammas).
The results are presented as design charts covering practical ranges of the slope angle, angle of internal friction, non-dimensional cohesion factor, edge distance, embedment ratio and horizontal seismic coefficient. The capacity factors increase with cohesion, friction angle and distance from the slope crest, and decrease with slope angle and seismic coefficient, whereas resonance of the soil layer produces the lowest capacities. For anchors beneath the slope face, the capacity is highest near the toe and decreases up the slope until a limiting edge distance is reached. The combined analysis yields higher capacities than the method of superposition, which becomes inapplicable when the corresponding cohesionless slope cannot remain stable under seismic loading. The stress proximity contours show that the capacity is governed by the shear strength of the soil and the confinement of the mobilised failure zone rather than by the extent of yielding alone.
The numerical databases were further used to develop artificial neural network and Gaussian process regression models. The fully optimised Gaussian process regression model gave the most accurate predictions for all four problems and was implemented as standalone executable tools for the rapid estimation of the capacity factors. The sensitivity analysis identified the non-dimensional cohesion factor as the most influential parameter for cohesive&ndashfrictional soils and the embedment ratio for cohesionless soil. The solutions, design charts and tools together provide a rational and safe basis for the seismic design of footings and anchors in hilly terrain.
